doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Tony Mottola as favorite guitarist and the thump rhythm
summary: Pallo names Tony Mottola as his favorite and describes his rhythm playing behind Johnny Mathis, the thump.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Yeah. Was there a turning point or a significant gig or a person that really made a difference early on for you. Can you point to a person or an event?
I really have to mention Tony Mottola, one of my favorites, besides Les Paul of course, who I work with. But Tony Mottola was the king to me. I just loved the way he played.
He could play anything, and may he rest in peace. He was a super, super, great guy.
And was he a good reader?

He had this, there was a nice sort of genre of instrumental music. I know my parents had his records, so I heard him growing up in the late fifties. It was sort of a very nice arranged thing featuring the guitar.
And I sort of miss that these days.

I do too. Because he would play chord melody, he’d play single note melody and of course he would play, if you listen to Johnny Mathis you’ll hear the first thump— I don’t know if Bucky Pizzarelli ever told you that — what we call the thump on the rhythm, and that’s how Johnny Mathis’ records, that was Tony Mottola playing rhythm. Unbelievable. Because guitar, if you play a record, we call a record, CDs today, when you played a record and you’ll say, “Can you hear the guitar” to a layman. He’ll say, “I don’t hear a guitar.” But in the background that rhythm guitar, like with Basie, that makes the whole thing. And Tony would play that so perfect. He was the first one to have that thump, and we call it a thump, where you don’t actually hear the change but you do hear the change and it just fits with the rhythm section so pretty and so perfect.
